statement: In people who use classic psychedelics, feeling safe and supported is associated with fewer reported difficulties in retrospective surveys, while the only prospective study among these sources found only a weak, uncertain link for the place and the people. In that study (Haijen et al., 2018; about 198 self-selected adults who planned an experience on their own initiative), a good feeling about the people who would be present and about the place, rated within the day before, went with slightly lower Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores rated about a day after (standardized beta −0.14, p = 0.070, not statistically significant), and with slightly higher well-being two weeks later (1.2 points on the well-being scale per standard deviation of the rating, p = 0.037, one of many coefficients in a model without correction for multiple tests; not significant at four weeks, p = 0.077); a retreat or a setting designed for therapy, reported afterwards in two yes-or-no questions that the authors combined into one variable, showed no statistically significant association with any acute measure (0.02), and the authors note that the term was not defined for participants. In an international online survey of 6,877 self-selected people who had drunk ayahuasca, each point higher on a 1-to-4 rating of support and safety at their last ceremony went with 0.29 points less extreme fear or panic on a 0-to-10 scale (95% CI 0.15 to 0.43, editors' calculation), slightly fewer difficulties in the weeks after, and current distress lower by 0.62 points on the 40-point Kessler scale, under 2 points across the whole rating (editors' arithmetic), after adjustment for age, sex, education, mental-health diagnoses, times drunk and years since the last drink and for the motivation, ceremony and other support variables; the ratings were made looking back by the same people, and averaged near the top of the scale (Perkins et al., 2021). Among 613 US adults in an online panel who had used a classic psychedelic, those who blamed a lack of psychological support for their most challenging experience rated it as more challenging (beta 0.25) and more often reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others in the days or weeks after (odds ratio 2.85, 95% CI 1.27 to 6.42, adjusted only for the other circumstances respondents could tick; 41 of the 613 reported any); blaming a disagreeable physical environment went with a smaller difference in challenge (0.09) and no detectable difference in harm thoughts, and blaming the people around with no statistically significant difference in either (odds ratio for harm thoughts 0.33, 0.11 to 1.01, p = 0.051, lower if anything) (Simonsson et al., 2023). Among 163 experienced people recalling two experiences, mostly at home or at a friend's house, those whose experience was at a party, club or festival (24 first and 12 most recent experiences) had higher average challenge scores than the rest (19 against 17 and 31 against 16 per cent of the maximum), a comparison the authors did not test (Palmer and Maynard, 2022). An opinion piece by the same group as the prospective study (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018) previewed, without methods, preliminary models from what appears to be an earlier cut of the same survey (266 people who completed four surveys), in which a 'therapeutic setting' (how it was recorded is not given) went with more peak or mystical-type experiences and trust in the people who would be present, rated beforehand, with less challenging ones; in the prospective study above, which appears to be the fuller report, a similar rating of the people and the place showed only a non-significant trend and a retreat or therapeutic setting no statistically significant association, so the preview is not counted as a further study and its figures are not used. No study read here put people in different places or company on purpose to compare them. The same opinion piece states that, by 2018 and apart from a dose study, retrospective analyses and one 1969 study, controlled studies isolating contextual factors had not been done, and a systematic review of 25 trials of classic psychedelics for psychiatric disorders other than substance use disorders, published up to December 2023, found no trial that compared settings (Estric et al., 2025; the trials were not appraised); in those trials, 12 kept two staff in the room throughout the session and five, published in 2023, one per participant, and rooms ranged from a hospital room left unchanged (4 trials) to one disguised as a living room or decorated, a choice the review's authors judged to have been made without evidence. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: In surveys, people who felt safe and supported during a trip reported a little less fear and fewer difficulties, but they rated both afterwards. The only study among these that asked people beforehand found only a weak, uncertain link between feeling good about the place and the people and how the trip went, and no detectable difference for retreats or settings designed for therapy. No study put people in different settings on purpose to compare them: a review of 25 clinical trials found none that did, and the trials set up their rooms and staff in very different ways.
population: People who use classic psychedelics outside laboratories: adults who planned an experience on their own initiative (one prospective study), people who drink ayahuasca (one international survey), a US online panel and a self-selected survey of experienced people
exposure: The place and the people: feelings about the setting rated the day before; a retreat or therapeutic setting; support and safety at an ayahuasca ceremony rated afterwards; lack of support, a disagreeable place or disagreeable company blamed for the most challenging experience; party, club or festival settings
comparator: People who rated the setting less favourably, did not blame it, or used elsewhere, within each study
outcome: Challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire), extreme fear or panic, difficulties in the weeks after, thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others, and current distress (Kessler-10)
magnitude: Haijen et al. (2018): setting component and challenging experience beta −0.14 (p = 0.070); setting component and well-being at two weeks 1.2 points per standard deviation (p = 0.037; at four weeks p = 0.077); retreat or therapeutic setting 0.02 (p = 0.81). Perkins et al. (2021), per point of a 1-to-4 support-and-safety rating: extreme fear (0 to 10) −0.29 (95% CI −0.43 to −0.15, editors'), integration difficulties −0.13, Kessler-10 −0.62 (under 2 points across the whole rating); the paper does not say which outcomes were modelled as ordinal, so reading −0.29 as points on the fear item assumes a linear model. Simonsson et al. (2023), attributions of the most challenging experience, adjusted only for the other attributions: no support beta 0.25, harm thoughts or attempts OR 2.85 (1.27 to 6.42); disagreeable physical environment 0.09, OR 0.88 (0.33 to 2.35); disagreeable social environment not associated, OR 0.33 (0.11 to 1.01, p = 0.051). Palmer and Maynard (2022), untested: party settings 19.27 against 16.77 (first) and 31.46 against 16.16 (most recent) per cent of the maximum CEQ score.

risk_of_bias.note: Retrospective ratings or attributions made by the same people at the same sitting as the outcome, in self-selected samples, with little or no adjustment (very high risk: sc_perkins_2021, sc_simonsson_2023, sc_palmer_2022); the prospective study is at high risk (confounding, heavy attrition) and its retreat item was undefined (sc_haijen_2018).

inconsistency.note: The direction differs by aspect: support and safety went with fewer difficulties in two retrospective surveys, but blaming the people around showed no association with challenge (and, if anything, lower odds of harm thoughts) in the panel survey; in the prospective study the setting rating showed only a non-significant trend in the same direction, and a retreat or therapeutic setting no association.

indirectness.note: Worded for the people and settings studied.

imprecision.note: Large surveys; the prospective coefficient's interval includes zero, which the statement says.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down two for risk of bias and one for inconsistency, giving very low (the floor). Status mixed: four independent studies; support and safety went with fewer difficulties in two retrospective surveys (Perkins et al.; the no-support attribution in Simonsson et al.) and the untested party comparison points the same way, but blaming the people around showed no such link, and the one prospective study found only a non-significant trend for its setting rating (and a weak link with well-being two weeks later) and no association for a retreat or therapeutic setting; recall at the same sitting may explain part of the difference, but no study has shown that it does. Two further sources change neither the certainty nor the status: an opinion piece from the same group (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018), whose preliminary survey figure appears to come from an earlier cut of the prospective study's sample and gives no methods, is not counted (opinion pieces are not evidence for empirical claims, METHODS §3.2), and the associations it showed for trust and a therapeutic setting were not significant in the fuller report; a systematic review of how 25 psychiatric trials reported set and setting (Estric et al., 2025; AMSTAR 2 critically low; a map of reporting, not of effects) found no trial comparing settings up to December 2023. A trial analysis in which the quality of the therapeutic alliance correlated with emotional breakthrough and mystical-type experience (Murphy et al., 2022), cited by that review, has not been read.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether music played during a psychedelic session changes how it goes or what follows: no study read here compared sessions with and without music, and the one randomized comparison of two kinds of music, in 10 people, found no detectable difference, with intervals too wide to rule one out. In an open-label trial of psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression (Kaelen et al., 2018), 19 patients each had two psilocybin sessions lying with eye-shades in a furnished room in a clinical research facility, with two therapists and one standard playlist (one patient who strongly disliked it in the first session heard a different playlist in the second). In interviews a week after the second session, 18 of 19 described welcome influences of the music (it intensified the experience for 17, guided 15 and calmed 10) and 10 of 19 unwelcome ones (it intensified feelings they did not want, or felt uncomfortable or irritating); 9 resisted where the music was taking them and 6 felt misguided by it, mostly by music that clashed with what they were going through. Four researchers' ratings of how much each patient had liked the music, resonated with it and been open to it, made from those interviews, correlated with the fall in self-rated depression recorded at the same time point, a week after the second session (liking r = 0.60, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.83; resonance 0.59, 0.19 to 0.82; openness 0.57, 0.16 to 0.81; editors' intervals), while the patients' own rating of how intense the drug had been did not (r = 0.004, −0.45 to 0.46). The music was rated after any improvement had happened, at the same time point, so patients who felt better may have described it more warmly; the three ratings were so closely related (r 0.90 to 0.96) that they probably measure one thing, agreement between the raters averaged r = 0.6 (the authors call this good), nothing was adjusted, and the authors say that without a placebo condition causal inferences are problematic. In a US online panel of 613 adults who had used a classic psychedelic, 30 (4.9%) named disagreeable music among the things associated with their most challenging experience; naming it was not associated with how challenging they rated the experience (standardized beta 0.05, p = 0.19) nor, with an interval too wide to tell, with thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others in the days or weeks after (odds ratio 2.67, 95% CI 0.87 to 8.21, with the other listed factors entered together), and 99 (16.2%) ticked changing the music among actions that had helped during it (Simonsson et al., 2023). In the one randomized comparison of music (Strickland et al., 2021; a published correction to the article has not been read), 10 adults who smoked (8 men; mean age 51), in an open-label pilot of psilocybin to help people stop smoking, each had one session with a Western classical playlist and one with an 'overtone-based' playlist of instruments such as singing bowls, gongs and didgeridoo, in random, counterbalanced order, wearing an eye mask and headphones, with a lower dose in the first session than in the second for all but one (study conditions; the analysis adjusted for dose). Mystical-type scores (MEQ30, self-rated at the end of each session and printed on a 0-to-1 scale) averaged 0.68 with the overtone playlist and 0.52 with the classical one, a difference of 0.16 (standardized 0.57; editors' 95% CI for the difference about −0.04 to 0.36, from rounded figures) that was not statistically significant (p = 0.107); Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores were almost the same (0.33 against 0.34; standardized difference −0.11, editors' interval about −0.73 to 0.51; p = 0.74). The data therefore fit anything from slightly lower to much higher mystical-type scores with the overtone playlist, and from a moderate fall to a moderate rise in challenge. About a quarter of the classical playlist's tracks were also on the overtone playlist, about an hour of each person's own chosen music was played in every session, the overtone playlist lost three tracks after the first three people, and everyone knew which music they heard. Six of the ten then chose the overtone playlist for a third session; smoking abstinence at the end of treatment (5 of 6 who chose it against 2 of 4 who chose the classical one; editors' Fisher p = 0.50) compares people who chose differently after hearing both playlists, so it cannot show an effect of the music. In a systematic review of 25 trials of classic psychedelics for psychiatric disorders other than substance use disorders, published up to December 2023 (Estric et al., 2025), 16 trials played a set playlist through headphones, one alternated music and silence, two allowed no music, and none compared settings; trials treating substance use, such as the smoking pilot, were outside its scope. An older study that compared five musical conditions, no music among them, during LSD sessions for alcohol use (Gaston and Eagle, 1970) is described by Strickland et al. as finding no significant differences, in a between-subject, partly non-random design without an objective clinical outcome; it has not been read here. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small study of 19 patients given psilocybin in a clinic, almost all said the music helped at times, and about half said it sometimes made things harder. Patients who spoke more warmly about the music had a bigger drop in depression, but both were measured at the same time, a week later, so feeling better may have coloured how they described the music. In a trial of 10 people, each heard classical music in one psilocybin session and music of gongs and singing bowls in another, in random order; how mystical or difficult the sessions felt did not clearly differ, but the trial was too small to rule out a real difference. None of the studies we read compared sessions with and without music.
population: Patients with treatment-resistant depression in an open-label psilocybin trial (19); adults who smoked, in an open-label psilocybin smoking-cessation pilot (10, with the order of two playlists randomized); and US adults who had used classic psychedelics in an online panel (613)
exposure: Music played during psilocybin sessions: one standard playlist (with one exception), as patients described it a week later; a Western classical or an overtone-based playlist, in randomized order within each person; disagreeable music named as associated with a most challenging experience
comparator: No study had a session without music: the other playlist in the same person (randomized comparison); patients who described the music less favourably; panel respondents who did not name the music
outcome: What patients said the music did; fall in self-rated depression (QIDS) one week after; mystical-type experience (MEQ30) and challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire) self-rated after each session; smoking abstinence by chosen playlist; thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others in the days or weeks after
magnitude: Kaelen et al. risk_of_bias.note: The randomized genre comparison has some concerns (card sc_strickland_2021): open label, self-ratings by participants who knew which music they heard, the overtone playlist changed after three participants, no registered analysis plan, and period effects untested. The music-experience ratings in the depression trial come from interviews at the same time point as the outcome, with no adjustment and no music-free condition (card sc_kaelen_2018, overall very high), and the panel survey's attributions are retrospective (sc_simonsson_2023); both are worded only as associations.

inconsistency.note: The sources answer different questions (two playlists compared, how patients experienced one playlist, music named in a survey).

indirectness.note: The randomized comparison tested two genres, not music against silence, with about a quarter of the classical tracks shared and each person's own music in every session, in 10 people in a smoking-cessation pilot; the other sources are a hospital trial of patients with depression and a US panel.

imprecision.note: 10 people in the randomized comparison, with intervals from slightly lower to much higher mystical-type scores and from a moderate fall to a moderate rise in challenge; 19 patients for the main correlation (interval 0.20 to 0.83); the panel's harm estimate for music rests on 30 people (interval 0.87 to 8.21).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; no registered analysis plan is reported for the genre comparison.

grade.reasoning: Rated from the one randomized comparison, the best evidence on whether the music itself changes a session: randomized evidence starts high; down one for risk of bias, one for indirectness and two for imprecision, giving very low (the floor). The correlational evidence on how patients experienced the music (Kaelen et al., 2018) is very low on its own, as before (low, minus two for risk of bias and one for imprecision). Worded as insufficient evidence because neither an effect of the music nor its absence can be shown with precision. Status single study: each question rests on one small study (two genres compared in 10 people; the music experience and the fall in depression in 19 patients); the panel survey adds only null associations, one very imprecise, for music named as associated with a difficult experience. A systematic review of 25 psychiatric trials up to December 2023 (Estric et al., 2025; AMSTAR 2 critically low) found none that compared settings, music included; trials treating substance use were outside its scope. A published correction to Strickland et al. (2021; doi 10.1021/acsptsci.1c00119) was not among the files and has not been read, so any figure it changes is unchecked. The only comparison with a no-music condition in psychedelic sessions that these sources mention, a 1970 quasi-randomized study of LSD sessions (Gaston and Eagle), is known only from Strickland et al.'s description and has not been read. A 2025 opinion article argues against music in therapy settings and notes that no controlled study compares music with silence; it has no card.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether music changes how a ketamine or esketamine session feels or how well the treatment works; one randomized trial found a smaller rise in blood pressure with music. In that trial (Greenway et al., 2024; Montreal, 2021 to 2022; registered), 32 patients with treatment-resistant unipolar or bipolar depression, accepted for a clinical course of six intravenous ketamine infusions over 4 weeks (treatment conditions), were randomly assigned to curated music throughout each 40-minute infusion (15) or to usual care without music (17). Across 181 infusions, systolic blood pressure rose from the start to the end of each infusion by 7.4 mm Hg less with music than without (95% CI 2.9 to 12.0; a mean rise of roughly 11.5 against 18.5 mm Hg, read from the figure), while diastolic pressure did not differ detectably (0.8 mm Hg less; the printed interval, −1.59 to 3.18, appears to have its signs transposed); no serious adverse events were recorded. The letter reports nothing on how the sessions felt, dissociation or depression (left for later papers), nor how many patients in each group needed treatment for raised blood pressure (the authors cite up to 20% of patients on intravenous ketamine for depression in general); the comparison was with no music, without a sound or attention control, so the music cannot be separated from attention or expectation; and one patient given usual care was left out of the analysis without a stated reason. Before that trial, as described in one scoping review (Kheirkhah et al., 2024; searched to December 2023; the included studies were not appraised, so its figures are second-hand), 14 studies of music with ketamine had been published, all in patients in clinical or trial settings. In nine, ketamine was given with other sedatives or painkillers, during procedures or, in one study, air medical transport; in most of them music went with less sedation or drug use and lower anxiety, pain or fear, but one trial found no effect on emergence reactions and another found more dreams or emergence reactions with music, though no unpleasant dreams, against 10 controls with unpleasant dreams. Of the five studies of ketamine or esketamine alone, only one compared people who listened with people who heard nothing: in 46 children having heart catheterization under ketamine anaesthesia, the 23 who heard recordings of their mothers' voices (musical in 12 of them) had less anxiety before the procedure and fewer emergence reactions than 23 who wore headphones with no recording. The other four were case reports and interview studies without such a comparison: a woman on esketamine nasal spray found that music of her choice helped with dissociation, confusion and anxiety; two patients with bipolar depression tolerated dissociation better with preferred music in later infusions, which may reflect getting used to the infusions; in 12 people given ketamine in a trial for alcohol use disorder, everyone who listened to music heard it distorted in speed and pitch, felt as good or bad depending on their state; and in 17 people on oral esketamine for depression, music was described as blocking distractions and helping inner exploration, but some felt it kept them tied to the outside world and one stopped using it. Up to its search, the review found no study comparing music with no music during ketamine or esketamine treatment for depression, and its own limitations say no conclusions can be drawn. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one trial of 32 patients with hard-to-treat depression who had ketamine through a drip in hospital, the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less in those picked at random to hear music than in those who heard none. The trial has not yet reported how the sessions felt or whether depression improved. An earlier review found 14 studies of music with ketamine, mostly with other medicines during surgery or tests, where music often went with less worry or pain; it found no study comparing music with no music during ketamine treatment for depression. So it is not known whether music changes how a ketamine session feels.
population: 32 patients with treatment-resistant unipolar or bipolar depression receiving a clinical course of intravenous ketamine in Montreal (one randomized trial), and patients given ketamine or esketamine in clinical settings (anaesthesia, sedation, depression and alcohol-use-disorder treatment) in 14 earlier studies gathered by a scoping review
exposure: Curated music throughout each 40-minute ketamine infusion (trial); music (or, in one study, recordings of mothers' voices) before, during or after ketamine or esketamine (review)
comparator: Usual care without music (trial); no music (headphones with no recording, or a blank soundtrack) in most procedural trials and in the one comparison of ketamine alone; no comparison in the case reports and interview studies (review)
outcome: Rise in systolic and diastolic blood pressure from the start to the end of each infusion (trial); anxiety, pain, emergence reactions, sedative use, dissociation and how the session was experienced (review)
magnitude: Greenway et al. (2024), randomized, 181 infusions in 32 patients (31 apparently analysed for the primary outcome, editors' inference from the flow diagram): change in systolic blood pressure from 0 to 40 minutes, music against no music, β −7.4 mm Hg (95% CI −12.0 to −2.9), P = .008; diastolic β −0.8 mm Hg (printed 95% CI −1.59 to 3.18, an interval centred on +0.8, so its signs appear transposed), P = .58; read approximately from the figure, mean systolic rise about 11.5 mm Hg with music and 18.5 mm Hg without; no clinical, experience or depression outcome reported. Kheirkhah et al. (2024): no pooled estimates. 14 studies: 9 with other sedatives (music with less sedation and lower anxiety or pain in most; no effect on emergence reactions in one; more dreams or emergence reactions in another); 5 with ketamine or esketamine alone, one comparing listeners with children who heard nothing (46 children: mothers' voices against headphones with no recording), the rest case reports (3 patients) and interview studies (17 and 12 people). No study comparing music with no music during ketamine treatment for depression up to December 2023.

evidence.extracted: Only blood pressure is reported; secondary outcomes are to be published elsewhere. The introduction cites up to 20% of patients receiving intravenous ketamine for treatment-resistant depression as needing medication for treatment-induced hypertension (from a 2021 expert review), but the number treated in each group is not given. The authors present music as a practical, low-risk, non-drug way to improve the blood-pressure response and name the modest sample as a limitation.

risk_of_bias.note: The trial (card sc_greenway_2024), RoB 2 some concerns: open label by necessity; sequence generation and allocation concealment not described; one usual-care patient excluded from analysis without a stated reason; more infusions missing without music (8 against 3), handled by inverse-probability weighting; who measured blood pressure, and whether they knew the group, not described. The review's studies were not appraised by the review and cannot be appraised here, and its highlights state benefits that its limitations disclaim (card sc_kheirkhah_2024).

inconsistency.note: Directions vary between the review's procedural trials (one null, one with more dreams or emergence reactions), as the statement says; the trial measured a different outcome.

indirectness.note: For the question asked (how a session feels, or how well treatment works), the trial reports only blood pressure, and its comparison was no music without a sound or attention control; the review's evidence is second-hand (METHODS §6.3) and mostly from ketamine given with other sedatives during procedures, often in children, and the only controlled ketamine-alone study used mothers' voices, partly spoken.

imprecision.note: One trial of 32 patients (interval for the smaller systolic rise 2.9 to 12.0 mm Hg); for how sessions feel, only small studies, mostly without a comparison group.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; the trial was registered (NCT04701866), but its registry record and protocol supplement were not read, so the reported outcome was not compared with the registered one.

grade.reasoning: The best evidence is now one randomized trial, which starts high, but it answers only blood pressure: on its own, the smaller systolic rise with music would rate low (high, minus one for risk of bias and one for imprecision). For how a session feels, the evidence is still the review's small, mostly procedural studies seen second-hand (low, minus risk of bias and indirectness, giving very low). Rated for the claim as worded: down one each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, giving very low. Status single study: one randomized trial for blood pressure, and, for ketamine or esketamine alone, one comparison of listening with not listening (46 children under anaesthesia hearing recordings of their mothers' voices), seen through one review. The claim no longer rests only on a narrative review; its new anchors still need a second reader's check. The trial's secondary outcomes, deferred to later publications, have not been seen.
